🛡️ Staying Safe & Compliant · Lesson 4 of 4

Kenyan Law for Creators: Data, Cybercrime & Disclosure

6 min read · Updated November 2026 · Free · Written for Kenya
Share: WhatsApp X Facebook Telegram LinkedIn

A Nairobi lounge was fined KES 1.85 million for posting a customer's photo on its social media without consent. The same rules apply to your page.

Most creators think law is a big-company problem. But Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 applies to anyone who collects or uses other people's personal data, and on social media that includes faces, phone numbers and customer lists. Here are the basics in plain English. It isn't legal advice, so check anything serious with a lawyer.

KES 9.375M
in ODPC fines across three Kenyan cases, including Casa Vera Lounge (customer photos) and Roma School, KES 4.55M for posting pupils' data online (HapaKenya, Dec 2025)

Data Protection Act: what touches creators

  • Faces are personal data. Posting a customer, a client's child or a reveller needs their consent. Kids need a parent's consent.
  • Marketing needs consent and an opt-out. Adding people to a WhatsApp broadcast or SMS list to sell to them needs their consent, notice, and an easy way to stop.
  • Registration with the ODPC is usually exempt below KES 5 million annual turnover and fewer than 10 staff. Some sectors, including education, health and direct marketing, must register whatever their size.
  • Penalties can reach KES 5 million or 1% of annual turnover, whichever is lower.
📋 Consent message before posting a customer
Hi [Name]! Thank you for coming to [Business]. We'd love to share your photo/video on our Instagram and TikTok. Is that okay with you? Reply YES to agree. You can ask us to take it down any time.

Cybercrime law: on your side, and watching you

Kenya's Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes (Amendment) Act 2025 extends penalties for phishing (fake calls and emails), clarifies identity theft to cover misuse of SIM cards and digital wallets, and widened cyber-harassment (in July 2026 the High Court struck down two of the new clauses, including the 'likely to cause suicide' wording, but harassment, phishing and identity-theft offences still stand). That helps you report scams. It also means a pile-on, a doxx or a 'name and shame' post can carry legal risk.

Advertising and disclosure

  • Paid or affiliate posts: say so plainly in the post. The US FTC's widely copied principle is that disclosure is the influencer's responsibility, and you can't assume followers know.
  • Gambling: the Betting Control and Licensing Board's guidelines (June 2025) bar influencers and content creators from promoting gambling at all.
  • Honest numbers: never present boosted followers or views to a brand as organic. That's a misrepresentation problem, not just a platform one.
✗ MYTH

If it's my phone and my page, I can post what I filmed.

✓ REALITY

Owning the camera doesn't give you consent. Casa Vera's own social pages earned it a KES 1.85M fine, and the ODPC said businesses should get customers' approval before posting.

✅ Do this today
⚡ Quick check

Why was a Nairobi lounge fined KES 1.85 million by the Data Protection Commissioner?

Casa Vera Lounge posted a patron's photo without consent. Under the Data Protection Act, faces are personal data, so get a 'YES' before you post anyone.

🧠 Key takeaways
  1. Faces and phone numbers are personal data. Get consent before you post or market.
  2. Small creators are usually exempt from ODPC registration, but not from consent rules.
  3. The 2025 cybercrime amendments cover phishing and SIM or wallet identity theft, and they also cover harassment.
  4. Disclose paid and affiliate posts, avoid gambling promotion, and never pass off boosted numbers as organic.
